name: Shillelagh
summary: A Python library and CLI that lets you query APIs, files and in-memory objects with SQL, by exposing each one as an SQLite virtual table; it is how Apache Superset reads Google Sheets.
intro: Shillelagh is a Python DB API 2.0 driver built on SQLite, through the APSW library. A table name is a URI in double quotes: a Google Sheets URL, `s3://bucket/file.parquet`, a path to a CSV file, a JSON API endpoint, a GitHub API URL or the name of a pandas DataFrame. For each one it creates an SQLite virtual table backed by an adapter, a Python class that knows how to read that source. SQLite parses and plans the query, and the adapter fetches the rows. One query can join several sources, for example a Google Sheet with a weather API, and write the result to a CSV file.

Each adapter declares its columns and which filters it can handle on each one, such as equality or ranges. When a query has `WHERE time >= '2026-01-01'`, Shillelagh passes that bound to the adapter, which turns it into an API parameter so the remote side does the filtering; an adapter can mark its filtering as inexact and let SQLite drop the extra rows. Adapters can also declare sort order, accept `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, and give the planner a cost estimate. The Google Sheets, CSV and S3 adapters support `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` as well, and `DROP TABLE` deletes the sheet, file or object. Other built-in adapters read HTML tables on web pages, Datasette tables, generic JSON and XML APIs, Socrata, WeatherAPI and the local machine’s CPU usage; third-party packages add Airtable, GraphQL and OData.

Besides the DB API there is a SQLAlchemy dialect (`shillelagh://`), a `gsheets://` dialect with only the Google Sheets adapter enabled, and a command-line shell. Apache Superset uses it for its Google Sheets and Shillelagh connections. Two experimental backends run the same adapters elsewhere: inside PostgreSQL as Multicorn2 foreign tables, and on sqlglot’s Python executor instead of SQLite. Version 1.4.5 came out in July 2026.
strengths: SQL, including joins across sources, over things that have no SQL interface, with nothing to run but a Python package
Filters are pushed into the API when the adapter supports it, so a `WHERE` clause becomes a request parameter instead of a full download
A standard DB API driver and SQLAlchemy dialect, so tools such as Superset can use it like any database
Writing a new adapter is a small Python class, and the docs walk through one step by step
limits: Runs in one Python process on SQLite: fine for spreadsheets and API responses, not for large datasets
Speed and filtering depend on each adapter; the generic JSON adapter, for one, downloads everything and filters on the client
Table names that carry credentials end up stored in a database file, so the docs advise using an in-memory database
Mostly one maintainer’s project; the Postgres and sqlglot backends are still experimental

story: Beto Dealmeida started working on Apache Superset in 2017. Superset can talk to any database that speaks SQL, and one of the most common requests he got from users was to read data kept in Google Sheets: in his words not a good database, but a friendly place to type data in. In 2018 he published gsheets-db-api, a DB API driver and SQLAlchemy dialect for Google Sheets.

Shillelagh generalised it. Instead of a driver for one service, it used SQLite’s virtual tables to put SQL in front of any source an adapter could read, with filters passed down to the API. Version 0.1 came out in October 2020, and 0.2 in February 2021 added the DB API, the SQLAlchemy dialect and the Google Sheets adapter as a drop-in replacement for the old `gsheets://` dialect. Version 1.0 followed in August 2021, and the gsheets-db-api README now tells users to switch. The name is an Irish wooden club: the docs picture “a leprechaun hitting APIs with a big stick so that they accept SQL.”

Superset adopted it for its Google Sheets connection, and Preset, which sells hosted Superset and published his write-up, ships a customised version with only the Google Sheets adapter. Later releases added a PostgreSQL backend on Multicorn2 (1.3, October 2024), an experimental sqlglot backend and a dialect for dbt’s MetricFlow (1.4, July 2025).

choices.why: SQLite already parses, plans and executes SQL, including joins and aggregates. Adapters only have to produce rows, so a new source costs a small class instead of a query engine.
APIs often can filter or page server-side. Letting each column declare the filters it accepts means a `WHERE` clause becomes request parameters instead of downloading everything.

choices.choice: A standard DB API driver and SQLAlchemy dialect
choices.why: Superset and other Python tools already speak SQLAlchemy, so any adapter becomes a database they can connect to without new integration code.
